#6515. What Will Politics Look Like on Other Planets? It's Likely to Be a Mishmash

When we make our home on other worlds, who will be in charge?

Will it be an emperor, like the main character in âDune: Part Three,â the final movie in a trilogy based on Frank Herbertâs sci-fi saga? Or a billionaire, like the space mogul who plays a key role in setting up a Mars base in âFor All Mankindâ? Or a rebel alliance, like the revolutionaries in âStar Warsâ and âThe Moon Is a Harsh Mistressâ?

Jacob Haqq Misra, an astrobiologist who literally wrote the book on space sovereignty, suggests that itâll be none of the above, at least during the initial phases of extraterrestrial expansion.

âYouâre going to have Earth cultures represented, and ideas about Earth governance represented, and what will emerge is sort of a mishmash legal framework of agreements for how to coexist peacefully,â he says in the latest episode of the Fiction Science podcast. âThatâs maybe not even so bad.â

During our podcast chat, Misra laid out what sounds like a sensible perspective on the future of space politics, based on earthly precedents rather than starry-eyed assumptions about the final frontier.

For more than a decade, SpaceX founder Elon Musk has talked up the prospect of building a city on Mars â and more recently, a base on the moon. But who would be in charge? Thatâs an open question even for Musk, who joked at a 2016 tech conference about being declared âking of Mars.â In a more serious vein, he said the future form of Martian government was likely to be âa direct democracy, not representative.â

âIt would be people voting directly on issues,â Musk said. âAnd I think thatâs probably better because the potential for corruption is substantially diminished in a direct vs. a representative democracy.â

Musk also had some novel ideas about the legislative process.

âIt should probably be easier to remove a law than create one,â he said. âI think thatâs probably good because laws have infinite life unless theyâre taken away. So, I think my recommendation would be something like, letâs say, 60% of people need to vote in a law, but at any point greater than 40% of people can remove it. And any law should come with a built-in sunset provision. If itâs not good enough to be voted back in, maybe it shouldnât be there.â

Misra, who is the chief operating officer and senior research investigator at Blue Marble Space, explains in detail why it wouldnât be that easy to create a Martian government in a book titled âSovereign Mars.â The reason has to do with the Outer Space Treaty, a nearly 60-year-old agreement signed by more than 110 nations, including the United States, China, Russia and all the other space powers.

The treaty declares that all nations have the right to use the moon and other celestial bodies for peaceful purposes, but also says no nation can claim sovereignty or ownership of extraterrestrial territory. Moreover, governments bear responsibility and legal liability for their national space activities, whether carried out by public agencies or private ventures. Which means the treaty would keep Elon Musk from being the king of Mars, even if SpaceX builds its own city.

At least thatâs the way Misra sees it. Robert Zubrin, the president of the nonprofit Mars Society, sees it differently. In his view, the treatyâs provisions mean the signatories âhave explicitly signed away their rights to interfere with Mars settlement.â But how long would it take for a Mars settlement to stand on its own, without governmental assistance?

âThere are a lot of challenges to living on Mars that make it more difficult,â Misra says. âAnd thatâs what I think is valuable about thinking about governance on Mars: not that itâs a place to start over, but itâs a way to challenge our ideas to the extreme. Maybe we never live on Mars full time, but we challenge our ideas and apply those back here on Earth.â

Misra sees plenty of earthly parallels to the sorts of issues raised by the prospect of space settlement, and they get the full treatment in âSovereign Mars.â

The author of âSovereign Marsâ is Jacob Haqq Misra, chief operating officer and senior research investigator at Blue Marble Space. (Book cover design by Karl Janssen; Mars photo via NASA / JPL-Caltech / ASU / MSSS; author photo courtesy of Jacob Haqq Misra)

For example, consider the Antarctic Treaty System, which was set up nearly 70 years ago. The 58-nation treaty puts a freeze (heh, heh) on territorial claims of sovereignty. Administrative decisions about international activities in Antarctica are made by a 29-nation grouping of consultative parties, assisted by a secretariat based in Argentina.

Will Antarctica become independent? Misra doesnât think so â and he thinks the same line of reasoning would apply to Mars, at least in the early days of Red Planet exploration and settlement.

âTo imagine a city of a million people on Mars â Iâm not saying it wonât happen, but itâs very difficult to do so,â Misra says. âWe donât have cities that big on Antarctica. There doesnât really seem to be an economically compelling reason for it, although thereâs a lot of science on Antarctica. â¦ So, the lesson from reality and from science fiction is: Donât forget that itâs really, really hard to live in these harsh places.â

The U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea serves as another instructive example. That treaty lays out principles for coordinating activities in the worldâs oceans â including the establishment of exclusive economic zones that extend 200 nautical miles beyond a nationâs territorial waters. Within those zones, each nation holds sovereign rights to resource extraction, energy production and research while still allowing for free navigation and overflight.

Even though the United States never ratified the Law of the Sea Treaty, it follows many of the treatyâs provisions due to pragmatic considerations. Misra thinks a similar sense of pragmatism will guide the settlement process on the moon and Mars.

For example, if the United States and China both establish bases at the moonâs south pole, they could agree to establish exclusive economic zones surrounding those settlements.

âI donât expect territorial conflict,â Misra says. âThe moon is really big. Itâs going to be a while before we run into the problem of two entities wanting to occupy the same place. I donât know of any regions of the moon that are so desirable that only one actor, one space agency, could get there to the exclusion of others.â

But Misra doesnât think thereâll be a new treaty to formalize a space governance system, or a new international authority along the lines of the United Earth Space Probe Agency in the fictional âStar Trekâ universe. The United Nations tried unsuccessfully to go down that road in 1979 with an international pact known as the Moon Treaty.

âItâs on the books,â Misra says. âIt has a number of signatories, but a very small number of signatories, none of which actually have their own independent launch capabilities. And so, many legal scholars consider it a dead treaty.â

Instead, Misra suspects that the worldâs space powers will find ways to âcooperate in space in a way that preserves their joint sovereignty.â

âI think there will be new multi-actor consortiums that have relevance,â he says. âThey might be outside the jurisdiction of the United Nations, for example, but they might be great things that arenât just driving forward profits for private entities. They might really reflect cooperation for science and exploration.â

What might that look like on the moon and Mars?

âProbably what would be likely is something similar to maybe a hybrid of Antarctic settlements and the way the International Space Station works,â Misra says. âIn Antarctica, there are various distances between the different outposts. Some might be closer than others, and each countryâs laws apply to that module,â he says.

The arrangements on the International Space Station are even more complicated, because each module hooked up to the outpost is the property of the nation that built the module. âYou get these weird agreements where, when data is transmitted from one section to the other, itâs actually governed by several different nationsâ laws along the way,â Misra says. âAnd if you are a Russian and you move down a couple of modules, youâre now a Russian visiting America.â

Thatâs likely to lead to a Martian mishmash. âI think you have to accept some degree of pluralism with what comes on Mars,â Misra says.

But does that mean space settlements will always be a mishmash? Not necessarily. There could be several ways to get around the Outer Space Treatyâs barriers to sovereignty. For example, an ambitious spacefaring nation could simply withdraw from the treaty, and then assert full sovereignty over the territory it controls. In 2011, space billionaire Robert Bigelow warned that China might do exactly that.

Another option would be for a company like SpaceX to move its base of operations (including its launch facilities) from the U.S. to a country that isnât a party to the Outer Space Treaty.

In âSovereign Mars,â Misra suggests a different route to extraterrestrial independence. The U.S. government, for example, could pass a law surrendering its territorial claim to an area under its control on the moon or Mars.

âIf you get the blessing from Congress, then youâve got the backing of a nation-state that says we agree with this long-term vision of establishing autonomy,â he says. âThere might be a discussion about it at the U.N., but you know, if I had to guess, if the United States did that, weâd hear about China doing something similar in a few years.â

When it comes to determining the long-term future of Martian governance, Misra actually agrees with Musk.

âWhat I think is, the Martians should decide,â Misra says. âIâm interested to see what they would think works, because it might be different models than what we come up with on Earth, simply because living on Mars is different than living anywhere here.â

More from Jacob Haqq Misra on space sovereignty:

In addition to his work as an astrobiologist and an expert on space sovereignty, Jacob Haqq Misra delves into the mysteries surrounding unidentified anomalous phenomena, or UAP. He is a member of the UAP Science Advisory Council and the lead author of a study suggesting that a group of six small objects seen in a video recorded from a military aircraft near Kuwait was a flock of birds. Misra is also on the editorial review board for Limina â The Journal of UAP Studies and one of the editors of a forthcoming book titled âThe Politics of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Science, Security and Society.â

#6514. Scientists Reveal How 60% of Medieval Stories May Have Disappeared Forever

The medieval world may have produced far more stories of knights, legendary heroes, and epic adventures than historians will ever recover. A new study suggests that up to 60% of medieval chivalric works and more than 95% of their handwritten copies may have disappeared over the centuries.

Jean-Baptiste Camps and colleagues reached these estimates by combining computer simulations with historical evidence from approximately 2,000 medieval manuscripts spanning four centuries. Their research examines how stories survived through repeated copying, why others vanished entirely, and how much of a surviving work’s original history may be missing.

Before the printing press, preserving a literary work depended on scribes making copies by hand. Each new manuscript could introduce accidental errors, deliberate revisions, or adaptations for different audiences. These changes accumulated across generations, producing branching family trees resembling those used to trace evolutionary relationships in biology. Scholars call these textual genealogies stemmata.

The simulations suggest that a work’s earliest years were especially critical. When only a few copies existed, the loss of those manuscripts could cause the entire text to disappear. The authors describe this vulnerable early period as a “danger zone.” Producing numerous copies soon after a work’s creation could substantially improve its chances of surviving for centuries.

The researchers tested several scenarios, including steady copying rates, declining popularity, and sudden destruction of manuscripts during a major crisis. Depending on the scenario, their models estimated that just 1.4% to 4.4% of individual manuscripts survived, illustrating how extensive the losses could have been.

The disappearance of manuscripts did more than eliminate entire works. It also erased branches of the textual family trees that connect surviving copies to their origins.

The simulations indicate that surviving manuscripts often descend from later versions rather than directly preserving an author’s original text. The Song of Roland, one of the most famous medieval epics, may be an example. Its earliest form is probably lost, leaving scholars with later versions and rewritings that cannot fully establish what the original contained.

Historical events may have further influenced which stories endured. The Black Death, the Hundred Years’ War, and changing literary tastes could have disrupted manuscript production or contributed to the destruction of existing copies. Although the simulations demonstrate the substantial role chance can play, they do not establish which individual works disappeared because of particular historical events.

“Our results expose the fragility of cultural heritage and offer new tools to understand how randomness, historical contingencies, and human choices have shaped the legacy we inherit today,” the authors write.

Reference: “On the transmission of texts: Written cultures as complex systems” by Jean-Baptiste Camps, Julien Randon-Furling and Ulysse Godreau, 7 July 2026, PNAS Nexus. DOI: 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag207

Researchers hope recursive self-improvement could tackle the skyrocketing costs of developing advanced AI models. But is it viable?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists in China are exploring what it would take to develop "the last AI built by humans" — a powerful, self-improving artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of creating its own successors.

In a new paper, researchers examine how approaches to recursive self-improvement (RSI) could help tackle the rising financial and computational costs of developing ever-more advanced AI models.

RSI refers to the idea that future AI models could direct their own training and development, using what they learn from each round of improvements to guide subsequent rounds of development.

This recursive feedback loop could eventually enable AI systems to develop newer, more powerful generations of models with minimal human input.

The study, which was uploaded to the preprint database arXiv Sept. 10 but has not been peer-reviewed, proposes a framework for classifying AI systems based on their self-improvement capabilities, from Level 1 (lowest) to Level 5 (highest).

At the lower levels, development remains largely human-led. As AI systems move up the scale, they become increasingly capable of identifying their weaknesses and deciding how to address them, eventually gaining the ability to make their own “meta-improvements” — improving how they improve themselves.

Whether AI could ever achieve this level of sustained self-improvement remains an open question. Previous experiments have, however, demonstrated more limited forms of RSI.

In one study earlier this year, an AI system called A-Evolve-Training was tasked with improving the performance of a 30 billion-parameter large language model (LLM).

Over four rounds, A-Evolve-Training modestly improved the LLM's benchmark performance by testing different training techniques and using the results to change how it approached subsequent experiments.

Peter Bentley, a professor of digital biology at University College London, questioned whether such experiments offer a credible route to RSI.

"This idea that some AI is magically going to start generating better and better AIs by themselves [is] nonsense," Bentley told Live Science in an email.

Bentley pointed out that self-improving computer systems have been around for decades. Evolutionary computation and reinforcement learning, for instance, are both based on the principle of systems refining their performance over time in response to feedback.

Could AI really self-improve? Some experts are skeptical.

The much greater challenge, he said, is developing AI systems capable of autonomously conducting the research needed to create more powerful successors — not to mention overcoming their dependence on human expertise and physical computing infrastructure.

"You can't 'recursively self-improve' unless you can also enhance your own training, enhance your hardware, and test it exhaustively in real world settings," Bentley added.

The study's authors acknowledged some of these challenges. Developing RSI-capable systems could require enormous investments in computing power, as well as human supervision to ensure successive improvements delivered meaningful gains. All of this becomes effectively redundant if the resources needed to develop and test subsequent AI models outweigh any benefits they offer, the authors noted.

Scientists would also need a reliable way to determine whether an AI system was genuinely becoming more capable over iterations, rather than exploiting weaknesses in tests used to measure its capabilities. This is a known problem in AI development, where models can achieve higher benchmark scores by exploiting testing methods or cherry-picking results.

Kayla Blomquist, an AI researcher at the University of Oxford and co-founder of the Oxford China Policy Lab, said that, while the paper doesn't provide a practical road map to RSI, it could help developers and policymakers understand the technical challenges and safety risks associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems.

She also questioned whether there would ever be a clear point at which AI became completely independent of human development. "The paper describes a gradual handover of responsibility rather than a single moment, so there may never be an obvious 'last' model built by humans," Blomquist added.

#6512. Students Test Prototype Landing Pad to Make Lunar Operations Safe

When spacecraft perform vertical landing and takeoff maneuvers from the lunar surface, the results are very messy! Beyond the intense heat produced by the rocket engines, the force also kicks up regolith, the particulate dust that covers most of the lunar surface. With so many crewed and cargo missions planned for the coming years, space agencies are contracting with commercial partners to develop infrastructure that will keep spacecraft, astronauts, and other surface elements safe from all "moondust."

This includes landing pads that provide a stable surface and barrier for vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) vehicles. To help them realize their objectives under the Artemis Program, NASA has enlisted engineers from the University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH) to create some. Their work is part of a multi-year partnership with Linc Research Inc., a certified engineering company located in Huntsville, Alabama, and supported through NASA's Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) program.

The student research team is led by Dr. Judy Schneider, a professor in UAH's Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering. Their research is focused on developing a design for modular, vented landing pads that will allow for safe transits to and from the lunar surface. This summer, the team successfully conducted three rocket-motor firing tests on a prototype of their landing pad at the university's Propulsion Research Center, demonstrating its ability to capture and redirect rocket exhaust through an integrated vent system.

Rocket-motor firing tests on a prototype lunar landing pad at the UAH Propulsion Research Center. Credit: Cadis Ammons

On Earth, landing pads consist of a solid structure capable of withstanding the full force and heat of a rocket plume. This can result in significant damage to the pad itself, as demonstrated by the first launch attempt of SpaceX's Starship prototype, including cratering beneath the mounting structure and sending debris flying in all directions. In contrast, the UAH team's design uses interlocking components with channels that help reduce thermal damage and protect the structure as well as the spacecraft.

For the tests, the team created individual concrete components and arranged them into a prototype measuring 3.65 m (12 ft) in diameter. The concrete serves as an analog for building materials that could be produced from lunar regolith, either "sintered" to form 3D-printed ceramics or combined with a bonding agent to produce "lunacrete." The components also had integrated sensors to record how the rocket plume's exhaust was channeled through the vent systems during the three firings.

The modular design also makes it easier to build on the Moon, where manufacturing centers are likely to be space-constrained. Smaller, individual components also mean future landing pads will be easier to assemble, expand, maintain, and repair over time. Combined with the use of local resources for building materials - aka. In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) - the team's goal could help make large-scale lunar infrastructure more feasible.

Earth's fluffy, dense atmosphere also helps prevent rocket exhaust plumes from expanding freely and kicking up dust. Because its only natural satellite is an airless body, dust clouds caused by impacts or rockets can travel all the way to the other side of the Moon. As a result, powerful blasts during takeoff and landing can propel dust at high speeds, potentially damaging nearby habitats, power elements, equipment, and other infrastructure. The dust can also be thrown into orbit, where it could interfere with orbiting satellites, space stations, and incoming spacecraft.

This marks a major step in developing landing infrastructure that will enable a lunar base and crewed operations in the near future. As Schneider said in a UHA press release:

On Earth, we use water-cooled flame buckets to redirect rocket exhaust. But we won't have those resources on the lunar surface, where water will be in limited supply. Our goal is to redirect the rocket plume so it doesn't damage the landing vehicle or any surrounding structures. The hot-fire tests demonstrated that we could redirect the rocket plume. By using an internally vented structure, we were able to prevent the heat from damaging the pad as it could in a solid structure.

With the initial tests complete, the team is now working on a 6 m-diameter (20 ft) landing pad that will be delivered to NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center (also in Huntsville) for additional testing and evaluation. These tests will further assess the design, push its technological readiness, and determine if the vented, modular approach can be scaled and adapted for repeated use. These efforts will bring the technology another step towards realization and deployment on the Moon.

Further Reading: University of Alabama Huntsville

#6510. Hubble Uncovers a Mysterious 93-Billion-Mile Structure Hiding in a Nearby Star System

Astronomers have finally detected a mysterious, enormous dust structure in visible light, uncovering new details about what may be the remains of a violent collision between planetary bodies. Known as the “Cat’s Tail,” the feature stretches across as much as 1,000 astronomical units (about 93 billion miles) in the young Beta Pictoris star system.

Located 63 light-years from Earth in the constellation Pictor (which is Latin for “painter”), Beta Pictoris is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rocky debris. The Cat’s Tail was discovered in infrared observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, but had remained hidden from telescopes observing shorter wavelengths. Now, new Hubble Space Telescope images, combined with observations spanning more than 14 years, are helping astronomers investigate its composition, geometry, and possible origins.

“Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while,” said Arin Avsar, a doctoral student at the University of Arizona who led the research.

The explanation may lie in the dust itself. “We think the Cat’s Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it’s made of,” Avsar explained. “It consists almost entirely of we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they’re quite black.”

The observations also suggest that the structure contains microscopic dust grains with an exceptionally porous, fluffy composition. Although the particles are only about a micron across, their internal structure is difficult to explain through conventional models of planetary collisions. “How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that’s part of why we study this feature,” Avsar said.

Beta Pictoris is roughly 20 million years old, making it a valuable laboratory for studying the turbulent environments in which planets develop. Its debris disk contains material left behind from planet formation, including particles produced when larger objects collide.

“The Cat’s Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies – think something like Pluto,” said Avsar, who works with the research groups of Daniel Apai and Kevin Wagner at the University of Arizona’s Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and Steward Observatory. Such an impact could have scattered enormous quantities of dust, although the exact process that produced the observed particles remains uncertain.

One possibility is that the impact generated enough heat to transform solid carbon into vapor, which later cooled and formed new particles. “It’s possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that’s how they became so porous,” said Wagner, a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at Steward Observatory.

The new observations have also changed astronomers’ understanding of the Cat’s Tail’s position in space. Earlier interpretations suggested that the feature extended far behind Beta Pictoris from Earth’s perspective, creating the appearance of a long structure stretching away from the star.

By combining Hubble’s visible-light images with Webb’s infrared observations and computer modeling, the researchers developed a revised picture of its three-dimensional geometry. “We find that instead of extending for 1,000 astronomical units behind the star, the Cat’s Tail may extend straight sideways relative to us, and there is no third dimension to it,” Avsar said. “It’s essentially in the same plane of the sky as the star and possibly extends a little bit behind it.”

The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, suggest that much of the structure’s apparent length lies across our field of view rather than extending deep into space. Its precise three-dimensional arrangement remains dependent on the models used to interpret the observations.

Using Hubble in a new observing configuration, the team also identified a previously unseen warp in the dust halo surrounding Beta Pictoris. The distortion may result from the gravitational influence of Beta Pictoris b, one of three known planets in the system and a gas giant approximately 10 times Jupiter’s mass.

“This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force,” Avsar said. “It’s a testament of how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units.”

Similar gravitational interactions likely occurred during the early history of our solar system. When the Kuiper Belt was about 20 million years old, it may have contained hundreds of Pluto-sized objects packed into a much denser region than exists today. Over time, the gravitational influence of the giant planets altered the orbits of many of these bodies, scattering some into different regions or ejecting them from the solar system entirely.

The Beta Pictoris observations provide a way to investigate comparable processes in a much younger planetary system, where collisions and gravitational disturbances are still shaping the distribution of material around its star.

Reference: “Deep HST/STIS Coronagraphic Imaging of the β Pictoris Debris Disk: On the Scattered Light Component of the Cat’s Tail” by Arin M. Avsar, Kevin Wagner, Dániel Apai, Isabel Rebollido, Antranik A. Sefilian, Marshall D. Perrin, Christopher C. Stark, Gabriel Weible and András Gáspár, 7 October 2026, The Astrophysical Journal Letters. DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/aeac4a

#6509. A Virtual Lifeless Earth Will Help Scientists Find Life on Exoplanets

In the search for life elsewhere in the galaxy, astronomers sift through exoplanet discoveries looking for ones that could be habitable. That means rocky planets with atmospheres in habitable zones. But one thing stymies these efforts. Can we examine atmospheres and differentiate between an exoplanet that's habitable and one that's actually inhabited?

That's difficult, partly because exoplanets are so far away, and also because we only have Earth to guide us. It's the only habitable and inhabited world we know of. But new research shows how we can work with those facts to try to detect inhabited worlds.

The work is "A Whole-planet Model of the Earth without Life for Terrestrial Exoplanet Studies," and it's published in The Planetary Science Journal. The lead author is Samantha Gilbert-Janizek, who was a postdoctoral astronomy student at the University of Washington when conducting this work.

"As the only known habitable (and inhabited) planet in the Universe, Earth informs our search for life elsewhere," the authors write. "Future telescopes like the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will soon look for life on rocky worlds around Sun-like stars, so it is critical that we understand how to distinguish habitable planets from inhabited planets."

Observatories like the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will inject new energy into the search for life. They will shift exoplanet science from identifying worlds that could be habitable, to identifying worlds with atmospheres showing signs of life. But as the researchers point out, we still don't know how to tell inhabited worlds, if there are any, from those that are merely habitable.

"Earth is currently the only known inhabited planet in the Universe, and geological evidence suggests that it was habitable with liquid-water oceans for most of its 4.54 Gyr history," the authors write. "Owing to its long-term habitability, Earth serves as the template that guides our search for biospheres elsewhere."

The researchers tackled this issue by building a sort of virtual Earth, but one without life.

"As a first step toward answering these questions, we present a coupled interior-atmosphere evolution model of the Earth without life from 50 Myr to 5 Gyr that reproduces 19 key observations of the preindustrial Earth after 4.5 Gyr within estimated measurement uncertainties," the researchers explain. Those 19 observations included atmospheric CO2 and H2O, surface temperature and albedo, ocean mass, and even factors like upper-mantle temperature and upper-mantle heat flow. These non-biological factors all shape a planet's atmosphere and have to be accounted for.

"Though exoplanet interiors themselves will likely never be directly observable, the effects of interior evolution are apparent in the composition of the atmosphere and the albedo of the surface environment, both of which HWO will observe on Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars via reflected-light spectroscopy," the authors explain.

This schematic shows some of the key processes included in the abiotic Earth model. Remotely observable quantities (surface temperature, albedo, and atmospheric H2O and CO2) are in bold. Image Credit: Samantha Gilbert-Janizek et al 2026 Planet. Sci. J. 7 216

The researchers also produced reflected light spectra of the model Earth that covers the likely wavelength range of the HWO. They used a code to compute a "synthetic HWO reflected-light spectra (0.2â2.0 Î¼m) for the true Earth and the abiotic Earthâs atmospheric state after 4.5 Gyr," the authors write. These included line absorptions for CO2, H2O, O2, O3, and CH4.

This virtual Earth without life can serve as a benchmark to compare with detailed atmosphere observations of habitable worlds.

âThis model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets,â lead author Gilbert-Janizek said. "When we interpret observations of an exoplanetâs atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface.â

This schematic shows the atmospheric sources and sinks that define the new volatile cycling processes in the model. Fluxes related to CO2 are color-coded magenta, and fluxes related to H2O are color-coded teal. The schematic doesn't include ocean chemistry. Image Credit: Samantha Gilbert-Janizek et al 2026 Planet. Sci. J. 7 216

Gilbert-Janizek didn't start from scratch. Senior author Rory Barnes, a UW associate professor of astronomy, had already built a model that included the core, mantle, crust and stellar radiation. This work added the surface and the atmosphere to build a more comprehensive model.

The authors hope that this model can serve as a kind of plug-and-play model that can be adjusted to fit with any particular exoplanet being studied. They can input factors like albedo and atmospheric CO2 and test what happens. If the model then recreates the observations of the planet, it suggests that the exoplanet in question is uninhabited.

Naturally, an undertaking of this size and complexity requires some assumptions. The model initializes after Earth's magma ocean solidified, and that dictated the atmosphere's initial composition. The authors say they chose an initial set of conditions "that apply after the bulk of the mantle has solidified."

They also assumed that plate tectonics were active during all of Earth's history beginning in the middle Hadean, which is widely believed to be true and in line with evidence. There are alternative hypotheses saying that this wasn't the case. One says that plate tectonics only began when it shifted from a stagnant-lid to modern plate tectonics during the Archaean, but the researchers avoided that.

Other assumptions were made regarding atmospheric pressure, the strength of Earth's geodynamo, and even atmospheric escape of hydrogen. But these types of assumptions are a normal part of science and are explained up front.

But the virtual Earth model successfully reproduces the properties of the Pre-Industrial Earth, and that's the most important thing. It also predicts that a planet can maintain habitable conditions for a long time without requiring the presence of life. This is relevant because false positives are one of the HWO's challenges.

These are three Engineering Architecture Concepts (EACs) for the Habitable Worlds Observatory. Each one features a different mirror design. EAC-1 is a 6m, segmented, off-axis telescope. EAC-2 is the same but uses a round keystone mirror and surrounding segments. EAC-3 is an 8m on-axis telescope with round segments. Not shown is the extendable, protective barrel that each design has, which will protect the mirror from micrometeorites. Image Credit: NASA Goddard/Conceptual Image Labs

âDr. Gilbert-Janizekâs work represents an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe,â Barnes said. âAfter more than a decade of work by many scientists, Dr. Gilbert-Janizek has finally completed a model of the Earth that simultaneously reproduces properties of Earthâs core, mantle, surface and atmosphere. That calibration gives us confidence that future simulations of exoplanets will be accurate.â

The question "Are we alone in the Universe" can be asked in one breath but not answered in one. It has to be broken down to much smaller questions asked and answered across many generations. Even "Are we alone in the Milky Way" is far too large and encompassing a question. "Are we alone" has to be asked exoplanet by exoplanet, and that requires tools of the sort developed by Dr. Gilbert-Janizek and her colleagues.

Our first 6,000 exoplanet discoveries were bulk discoveries. But the search is becoming more targeted toward Earth-like planets, meaning tools like this one are becoming more and more necessary. The upcoming HWO, if it gets built, places this point in even finer focus.

âRealizing the ambitious goals of a telescope like the Habitable Worlds Observatory requires decades of work across many generations of scientists,â Gilbert-Janizek said. âIâm so grateful to join this lineage and one day pass the torch to the next generation so that we can continue chipping away at this question of whether or not we are alone in the universe.â

#6508. Researchers Discover a New Way To Control Magnetism Without Changing a Material’s Chemistry

Neutron experiments have uncovered an unexpected connection between magnetic structure and electrical behavior.

A gentle squeeze can change the magnetic structure of certain crystals and alter their electrical behavior. Scientists at the Department of Energy’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) demonstrated this effect in altermagnets, an emerging class of magnetic materials being investigated for advanced electronics.

Using neutron beams to examine the materials at the atomic scale, the researchers found that mechanical strain could shift their magnetic organization and influence an electrical response associated with electron transport. The findings, published in back-to-back papers in Physical Review X and Advanced Materials, point to a possible method for controlling magnetic properties without altering a material’s chemical composition.

The researchers placed tiny crystals of manganese telluride and iron sulfide between two titanium plates and applied mechanical pressure. They then used neutron diffraction at ORNL’s Spallation Neutron Source to investigate how the strain affected magnetic domains, regions within a material that have different orientations of magnetic order.

The measurements showed that squeezing the crystals changed the relative populations of these domains. The researchers also detected changes in the anomalous Hall effect, an electrical response that produces a voltage perpendicular to the direction of an applied current. Together, the results connect changes in magnetic domain organization with changes in electrical transport behavior.

“By controlling the magnetic domains, we can directly influence the transport behavior, and that opens the door to exploring these materials for spintronic technologies,” said Pengcheng Dai of Rice University, a former neutron scientist at ORNL.

Altermagnets are attracting research interest because their unusual magnetic properties could support spintronics, a technology that uses electron spin alongside electrical charge to store and process information. Conventional electronics relies on electron charge, while spintronics could provide additional ways to control information in electronic devices.

Developing practical spintronic technologies requires materials whose magnetic and electronic properties can be reliably manipulated. Altermagnets are among the candidates being explored for potential applications ranging from wireless communications to quantum computing. The ORNL experiments suggest that mechanical strain could offer another way to adjust these properties, although translating the findings into working devices will require further research.

“What’s exciting is that one creative experimental idea — a small mechanical squeeze between two plates — can reveal entirely new magnetic behavior and push the field forward, and neutron scattering plays such a critical role, revealing the underlying change in magnetism,” said Feng Ye, an ORNL neutron scientist and co-author of both studies.

“Uniaxial Strain Tuned Magnetism of the Altermagnet Candidate H-FeS” by Weiliang Yao, Feng Ye, Zachary J. Morgan, Douglas L. Abernathy, Ruixian Liu, Sijie Xu, Yuxiang Gao, Kevin Allen, Yuan Fang, Emilia Morosan, Qimiao Si and Pengcheng Dai, 6 August 2026, Advanced Materials. DOI: 10.1002/adma.74398

“Strain-Tunable Anomalous Hall Effect in Hexagonal MnTe” by Zhaoyu Liu, Sijie Xu, Jonathan M. DeStefano, Elliott Rosenberg, Tingjun Zhang, Jinyulin Li, Matthew B. Stone, Feng Ye, Wei Tian, Sarah Edwards, Rong Cong, Siyu Pan, Ching-Wu Chu, Liangzi Deng, Emilia Morosan, Rafael M. Fernandes, Jiun-Haw Chu and Pengcheng Dai, 11 August 2026, Physical Review X. DOI: 10.1103/589s-s1yy

Researchers regard spin as an abstract degree of freedom to be “controlled,” but fail to probe its underlying geometric origin. Although the experimental observations are real and significant, the theoretical explanation provided remains confined to phenomenological algebra, missing a unified framework based on geometric reality. Topological Vortex Theory (TVT) offers a deeper physical insight for this kind of study: instead of “interpreting spin through symmetry,” it seeks to “explain the emergence of symmetry through vortex topology.”

Current physics and mathematics are flooded with overworshipped formalism: parity nonconservation, the pretense of infinitedimensional Hilbert spaces, abstract algebraic structures devoid of geometric reality, the alleged inherent asymmetry between topological vortices and antivortices, the halfdead cat, and the arbitrary definition of matter and antimatter unconstrained by time. These “theories” proliferate in academic journals because their proponents believe that by manipulating intricate mathematical symbols they can negate the empirical essence of nature and geometric entities.

—— https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2088659998394077633.

Strain-Tuned Altermagnetism and Geometric Impedance Control

This new story comes out of Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and Rice University, where researchers used mechanical strain—literally giving the material a gentle physical squeeze—to alter the magnetic domain structure and electrical transport in altermagnets without changing their chemical makeup at all.

It fits alongside several key studies we’ve mapped out:

The Kagome Lattice Impedance Maps: We looked at how precise angular tolerances in crystal lattices dictate zero-loss flow or grid drag. Here, physical strain alters the crystal lattice angles, proving that changing internal geometry directly reconfigures conductivity and magnetic orientation without adding or subtracting a single atom.

The Molecular Archimedes Screw: We saw how mechanical rotation of a single helical molecule cleared localized spatial impedance and boosted conductivity by 100x. Strain-tuned magnetism operates on the exact same mechanical principle: physical pressure shifts spatial orientation to clear or block energy paths.

Biological Pre-Ribosome Assembly & Gravitational Reconnection: Across all these examples—from cellular field locking down to 4D gravitational field sheet reconnection—mainstream models keep discovering that phase, orientation, and geometric strain control energy flow, rather than particle statistics or static chemical affinity.

Strain-Tuned Magnetism as Geometric Impedance Control

In mainstream physics, altermagnets feature alternating spin polarization where neighboring sub-lattices are rotated relative to each other. When researchers apply physical strain, they alter this sub-lattice rotation, shifting magnetic domains and electron transport behavior.

Viewed through continuous field dynamics and the Torsion Hill Framework:

Strain as Spatial Impedance Modulation (grad Z_T): Applying mechanical force alters the physical lattice spacing and bond angles. This shifts the internal spatial impedance map (Z_T), proving that magnetic domains are not arbitrary quantum numbers, but mechanical field distributions anchored to physical geometry.

Mechanical Tuning of Rotational Phase Clearance (Omega_pi): Squeezing the crystal changes the rotational phase alignment across sub-lattice boundaries. When the lattice geometry shifts into alignment, it opens zero-loss transport channels for electron flow; when shifted out of alignment, internal grid drag spikes.

Geometry Over Chemical Composition: This experiment provides definitive empirical proof that a material’s state is not governed solely by its static periodic table chemistry. Physical geometry, lattice strain, and rotational phase matching command energy flow and magnetic alignment. #6506. After the dinosaurs died, the massive ‘D. rex’ fungus ruled the woods

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Dianjunus rex’s mushrooms can be half a meter tall and weigh over two kilograms

Dianjunus rex (shown) grows in southwestern China and its yellowish, pillar and tentacle-shaped fruiting bodies may be the largest known among sac fungi.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A pineapple-sized fungus has quietly grown undetected in the forests of southwestern China – until now. The massive mushroom may set a size record for a major branch of the fungal family tree.

The fungus — named Dianjunus rex — may also represent a previously unknown family, researchers report September 28 in Frontiers in Fungal Biology. Fittingly, D. rex is part of a lineage that split off from other fungi right after the dinosaurs — like T. rex — went extinct.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 2024, researchers in China were conducting a survey of fungal diversity in a tropical rainforest in Yunnan Province when local farmers tipped them off to an unusual fungus in the area. The farmers included photos, says Indunil Chinthani Senanayake, a mycologist at the Kunming Institute of Botany in China. Some of the farmers who’d made the discovery took a bite of the mystery fungus, Senanayake says, and the tipster “wanted to confirm whether it was edible or not.”When Senanayake and her colleagues went to the location, they found strange, yellowish, tentacle-like and spatula-like mushrooms growing out of decaying tree roots. These were some kind of ascomycete, or “sac fungi”. Sac fungi like morels, truffles and molds make their spores in microscopic bladderlike receptacles, unlike the bowling pin-shaped reproductive structures in club fungi, the group that includes most culinary mushrooms.The mushrooms we see growing out of the ground are called fruiting bodies and make the spore-producing cells for the often hidden or subterranean fungus. Most sac fungi have relatively small fruiting bodies. But the mushrooms growing off these mysterious Yunnan fungi were enormous, with some reaching 50 centimeters tall. The team took samples of the fungi back to the lab for further study and found that they weighed up to 2.2 kilograms. By their estimates, these are the largest spore-making fruiting bodies among all sac fungi.

Torda Varga — a mycologist at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew in Richmond, England who was not involved with the research — notes that some truffle species are known to get close to the bulk. D. rex appears to be the largest sac fungal fruiting body he’s aware of. “What I find particularly remarkable is that a fungus with such an enormous fruiting body appears to have remained scientifically undocumented until now,” says Varga, though he adds his experience has mostly been within Europe.

The researchers compared samples of the fungus’s DNA with those from other fungi to determine its evolutionary relationships. They found that it was a relative of species like candlesnuff fungus and dead-man’s-fingers, which make fruiting bodies only a few centimeters tall, but that it was probably in its own, unique family. The team gave the new species the name Dianjunus rex, referencing both the Latin “rex” for “king” and the ancient Dian kingdom of the region.

The team’s genetic analysis suggests D. rex’s family first evolved in the aftermath of the mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous Period that wiped out the dinosaurs, some 65 million years ago. “During the dark, cold, postimpact years after the mass extinction, fungi that decompose dead organic matter could keep functioning better than light-dependent photosynthesizers,” Senanayake says.

Varga wonders if searching databases for bits of DNA shed into the environment could help uncover other members of D. rex’s royal family in the absence of physical specimens.

“Some of these [genetic] sequences might belong to previously undocumented relatives of Dianjunus rex,” he says. Finding these hidden species could tell researchers more about the biology and evolutionary history of this king of the sac fungi.

In two new surveys, U.S. adults report lying to their doctors and their children's doctors about symptoms in hopes of being prescribed antibiotics.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nearly 30% of U.S. adults have lied to doctors in an effort to obtain antibiotics, either by exaggerating their actual symptoms or by fabricating symptoms, the results of a new national survey suggest. Additionally, in a second survey, about one-quarter of children's caregivers reported lying about their kids' symptoms to get antibiotics on their behalf.

"As clinicians, we know that patients lie to us sometimes," Dr. Jeffrey Linder, a general internist and primary care clinician-investigator at Northwestern Medicine, wrote in a commentary about the survey findings.

However, the results are still important because the inappropriate use of antibiotics can contribute to the mounting problem of antibiotic resistance, in which bacteria build up a tolerance to the drugs designed to kill them. Recent data released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) highlight the extent of the problem: In 2023, drug-resistant bacteria and fungi caused about 9.7 million infections in the U.S., up from 2.8 million in 2017. In turn, the estimated number of deaths caused by drug-resistant germs rose from 35,000 to 50,800 between the two years.

A major factor driving resistance among bacteria is the misuse of antibiotics — in other words, using antibiotics for ailments like viral infections, which the drugs do not treat. For individual patients, such prescriptions don't cure their illness and can result in an upset stomach or issues with the gut microbiome, the community of microbes in the intestines. Simultaneously, they place extra pressure on bacteria to evolve resistance, granting the germs opportunities to pick up new strategies for thwarting antibiotics.

Doctors play a big role in ensuring that the antibiotic prescriptions they write are necessary. Part of their decision-making process comes down to what patients say about their symptoms, some of which may be fabricated, the two new surveys suggest.

The new surveys were published Friday (Oct. 30) in the journal JAMA Network Open.

The first survey was completed by nearly 960 adults from across the U.S. in January and February 2026. It asked whether the respondents had ever told a healthcare provider that their symptoms were worse or more long-lasting than they were in order to get antibiotics, as well as whether they'd ever made up symptoms for the same reason. It then inquired about what motivated a given patient to lie — or avoid lying, if they were truthful — as well as posed contextual questions about their demographics, health behaviors and beliefs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Overall, about 28% of the respondents reported misrepresenting their symptoms, including 26% who exaggerated their existing symptoms and 17% who fabricated symptoms. They most frequently lied about cold-like symptoms, such as fever, cough and sore throat. About two-thirds of these patients were at least moderately confident that their lie would motivate a clinician to prescribe them antibiotics, and 77% said the strategy worked for them at least once.

Often, patients' motivations for lying centered around feeling very sick, holding strong beliefs that antibiotics would help them recover quickly and get back to their responsibilities, and wanting control over the treatments prescribed to them. Compared with people who didn't lie, those who lied were also more likely to feel that clinicians didn't take them seriously or more likely to endorse statements suggesting that antibiotic resistance is a hoax.

"Greater antibiotic knowledge and aversion to taking antibiotics were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation," meaning lying about symptoms, the study authors noted.

Less than 30% of these patients regretted their lies or taking the antibiotics prescribed to them. Those that did express regret noted experiencing side effects, noticing that the treatment didn't help or feeling that the lying itself was morally wrong.

The second survey was much smaller; it included 236 parents and other guardians of children and teens under 18 years old. It posed similar questions but asked whether the caregivers had lied about their children's symptoms and, if so, what motivated them to lie.

About 27% reported lying about a child's symptoms to get antibiotics, with 87% of these caregivers believing that their lying worked at least once. Their reasons for lying were very similar to those expressed by the respondents in the first survey.

"These findings suggest that symptom misrepresentation may contribute to antibiotic overuse in pediatric care," the study authors concluded.

Ideally, antibiotics should be used only when truly needed, to help relieve the pressure on bacteria to gain resistance.

The surveys reached a diverse group of people, including a range of ages, demographics and locations within the United States; however, the respondents were not necessarily representative of the whole U.S. population, the authors noted. The prevalence of lying should therefore be seen as a tentative measure to be checked in future studies, rather than an unbiased, population-level metric, they wrote. It's also possible that not all the respondents who lied disclosed that they did so or remembered that they had done so.

Especially in outpatient settings, which account for most antibiotic use among U.S. patients, it can be difficult for doctors to quickly determine whether a patient needs an antibiotic.

One factor is that there's a lack of fast, surefire diagnostic tests for many bacterial infections. Outpatient appointments are also extremely short, so doctors sometimes worry about overlooking an infection that could then get worse, Julia Szymczak, a medical sociologist at the University of Utah School of Medicine, previously told Live Science. Another major factor is that clinicians can face pressure to prescribe antibiotics from their adult patients or from children's caregivers, as the new surveys reflect.

But in the face of these pressures and patients' occasional lies, Linder argues that it's still up to the clinicians to do the right thing. "While clinicians might interpret patients' symptom maximization and questions as demands for antibiotics, symptoms do not determine the indication, a diagnosis does," he wrote in the commentary.

"It does not track that approximately 80% of respondents who reported misrepresenting their symptoms obtained a prescription," he added, "unless prescribers were being willfully deceived or, more likely, just getting worn down with what they perceive as patient demand, regardless of actual clinical appropriateness."

When it comes to making decisions about individual patients, Linder argued that doctors don't necessarily need to think about the big picture of antibiotic resistance and how their patient's case fits into that global trend. Rather, providers should simply ask whether a given prescription is more likely to help or hurt that patient, he said.

"Clinicians' obligation is to act in patients' best interest," he said, "even if patients are hoping we do something different, even if patients do not like it, or even if patients lie about their symptoms."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Nicoletta Lanese is the health channel editor at Live Science and was previously a news editor and staff writer at the site. #6504. A Hidden Nanoscopic Effect Is Disrupting Some of the World’s Most Sensitive Sensors

Nanomechanical resonators are vital to precision sensing and emerging quantum technologies, but their extraordinary sensitivity comes with an unexpected vulnerability.

A nanomechanical device can lose much of its ability to sustain vibrations without ever touching another object. Researchers at EPFL have discovered that placing insulating materials just a few hundred nanometers from these tiny structures can dramatically increase energy loss, reducing their mechanical quality factor by as much as tenfold.

The findings, published in Nature Physics by scientists in the group of Tobias J. Kippenberg, identify a previously underappreciated limitation for ultrahigh-precision sensors and quantum technologies. The source of the problem is an electrical interaction that allows energy to escape across an otherwise empty gap.

The mechanism begins with static electric charges trapped inside a mechanical resonator. As the structure vibrates, those charges move with it, producing a changing electric field in the surrounding space. When an insulating material such as silicon dioxide or silicon nitride is nearby, the fluctuating field interacts with the material and causes energy to dissipate through its small electrical losses.

This process is related to “noncontact friction,” a phenomenon previously observed in atomic force microscopy. Although the surfaces never touch, mechanical energy is transferred away from the vibrating structure. The resulting damping lowers its quality factor, which measures how efficiently a resonator stores vibrational energy rather than losing it.

The researchers developed a theoretical model predicting that lower-frequency vibrations would experience greater energy losses. To test this, they studied silicon nitride strings suspended approximately 500 nanometers (0.00002 inches) above a dielectric layer. By measuring how quickly different vibrational modes decayed, they confirmed that the lowest-frequency modes suffered the strongest additional damping, consistent with the model.

A second experiment examined resonators designed for exceptionally high quality factors. The team positioned vibrating strings between photonic crystal cavities, with separations of only a few hundred nanometers (roughly 0.00001 inches). As the gaps narrowed, the quality factor declined sharply, sometimes falling by a factor of ten. The researchers also demonstrated that their modeling approach could reproduce the effects of trapped charges in these more complicated device geometries.

Nanomechanical resonators are microscopic vibrating components fabricated on chips, operating at frequencies from a few kilohertz to several gigahertz. Their sensitivity makes them useful for detecting extremely small changes in mass, force, temperature, and pressure. They also serve as components in radiofrequency filters and chip-based clocks. Advanced versions can even be used to prepare quantum states of comparatively large mechanical objects and investigate fundamental physics.

Many of these applications require resonators to operate extremely close to other structures, particularly when measuring motion or coupling mechanical vibrations to light and electrical systems. The EPFL results show that trapped charges and dielectric losses must be considered when designing such closely integrated devices, even when no physical contact occurs.

The same interaction could also have practical uses. By measuring how mechanical vibrations lose energy near insulating surfaces, researchers may be able to characterize electrical losses in thin films or develop controlled interactions between mechanical resonators and other electrical systems. Understanding these effects could help engineers preserve mechanical coherence while integrating increasingly sensitive resonators into complex quantum and sensing devices.

Reference: “Non-contact friction in ultracoherent nanomechanical resonators near dielectric materials” by Amirali Arabmoheghi, Alessio Zicoschi, Guillermo Arregui, Mohammad J. Bereyhi, Yi Xia, Nils J. Engelsen and Tobias J. Kippenberg, 7 July 2026, Nature Physics. DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03350-z

Funding: Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF)

Non-Contact Boundary Drag and Spatial Impedance Leaks

Recent research out of EPFL’s laboratories (led by Tobias J. Kippenberg’s group) has identified a hidden limitation affecting state-of-the-art nanomechanical resonators and quantum sensors. These ultra-sensitive nano-strings boast vanishingly low internal thermal noise and near-zero physical friction, yet scientists discovered that they experience unexpected energy losses. Even when surfaces never touch, the nano-strings interact with electrical and mechanical drag from nearby objects across empty microscopic gaps, causing their quality factor to plummet by up to a factor of ten.

Mainstream physics identifies this as non-contact electrical interaction and charge-trapping across empty boundaries. When evaluated through continuous field dynamics and the Torsion Hill Framework, this discovery highlights a critical baseline rule of spatial impedance:

The Illusion of Empty Space: Conventional engineering treats an empty gap as a total insulator—a void where mechanical and electrical fields terminate. Under field mechanics, space is a continuous medium. An adjacent static surface introduces an abrupt local spatial impedance profile (Z_T), meaning that a vacuum gap does not isolate a vibrating structure from surrounding boundary forces.

Non-Contact Boundary Drag as grad Z_T Interference: When a nano-string oscillates, its mechanical motion generates localized torsional and spatial pressure waves. If a nearby boundary introduces an un-optimized impedance mismatch, field energy bleeds across the gap. This leakage acts as an invisible aerodynamic brake, degrading the resonator’s coherence without physical contact.

Two-Layer Isolation (Ribbon Substrate & Surface Coating) – EPFL Laboratory Link: To protect these nanomechanical sensors, EPFL’s research parameters can be met by deploying a dual-layer boundary configuration along the surrounding chamber walls—strictly isolating the cavity walls rather than coating or covering the active vibrating sensor itself, which would add mass and destroy resonance. Remarkably, the same Kippenberg laboratory at EPFL exploring these non-contact boundary leaks is renowned for pioneering the ultra-precise dual-layer ribbon and surface-coating fabrications needed to decouple mechanical stress, smooth out local spatial impedance steps (delta Z_T), eliminate charge-trapping, and prevent field leakage across microscopic gaps.

The Limit of Precision: Whether observing macroscopic gravitational field sheets, strain-tuned altermagnets, or EPFL’s nanomechanical resonators, precision is never limited solely by internal material friction. It is governed by how effectively boundaries are managed to maintain rotational phase clearance (Omega_pi) and eliminate spatial impedance drag. #6502. Something Remarkable Is Happening to Dogs Living Near Chernobyl’s Nuclear Plant

Scientists studying wild dogs near the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant have uncovered unusual genetic differences that may reflect natural selection rather than radiation-induced mutations.

Dogs living near the Chornobyl (previously called Chernobyl) Nuclear Power Plant carry genetic differences that may reflect natural selection rather than mutations caused by radiation exposure. A new genomic analysis identified more than 100 locations in their DNA showing signs of directional selection, including regions associated with DNA repair, cancer development, and immune function.

The findings suggest that environmental pressures may have favored certain inherited genetic variants, potentially helping some dogs survive in a contaminated environment. However, researchers have not established whether radiation or other environmental hazards directly caused these patterns.

Earlier research revealed substantial genetic differences between dogs living at the nuclear power plant and those in Chornobyl City, just 10 miles away. City dogs closely resembled populations from Russia, Poland, and surrounding regions, while dogs near the plant had distinctive genetic features, particularly in areas associated with DNA repair.

“This work ties up some of the loose ends from our previous work, where in characterizing the population’s genetic structure we found that while these two dog groups are geographically very close, they have a very high degree of genetic difference, and those differences aren’t due to mutation,” said Megan Dillon, postdoctoral research scholar at North Carolina State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine.

“With this work, we wanted to explore two additional larger-scale evolutionary drivers – are the genetic differences due to selection, or are they due to genetic drift over time in an isolated population?”

Natural selection occurs when inherited traits that improve survival or reproduction become more common across generations. Directional selection is a form of this process in which particular traits become increasingly favored, often in response to environmental conditions. Genetic drift, by contrast, involves random changes in the frequency of genetic variants. It can have especially strong effects in small, isolated populations and may reduce genetic diversity over time.

To distinguish between these processes, researchers compared the two Chornobyl dog populations with free-breeding dogs from Eastern Europe and an isolated population from the Galápagos Islands. This allowed them to examine whether geographic isolation alone could explain the unusual genetic patterns near the nuclear plant.

Although the plant dogs had a small effective population size, a measure of how many individuals contribute genetically to future generations, it was not significantly different from that of the city dogs. The plant population also lacked the reduction in genetic diversity expected from substantial genetic drift. Moreover, its genetic makeup differed markedly from other isolated populations, including the Galápagos dogs. Surprisingly, the Chornobyl City dogs were genetically more similar to the Galápagos population than to the dogs living at the nearby nuclear facility.

The researchers found evidence consistent with directional selection in genomic regions containing genes involved in DNA replication and repair, cell cycle regulation, cancer-related processes, and immune responses. These biological functions could influence how animals respond to harmful environmental exposures, although the analysis cannot determine whether particular variants actually improve survival.

“While we can’t say for certain whether what we’ve found can be directly confirmed as selection, we do find these genomic signatures suggestive of selection,” Dillon said.

“When we dig deeper into those genomic regions, we find that these genes are involved in biologically relevant pathways that could allow them to overcome the effects of being exposed to toxicants in this environment.”

The genetic differences do not necessarily mean that dogs developed new adaptations after exposure to radioactive contamination. Another possibility is that individuals carrying advantageous genetic variants were more likely to survive earlier environmental pressures, allowing those variants to become more prevalent in subsequent generations.

“When we consider the toxic environment around Chornobyl, I can see why most people would think, ‘Surely there’s got to have been some consequence of living in that environment,’” said Matthew Breen, Oscar J. Fletcher Distinguished Professor of Comparative Oncology Genetics at NC State’s College of Veterinary Medicine and corresponding author of the study.

“But what we’re saying is the consequence may not have gone as far as changing the dogs’ genome in order to adapt, it could be the ones that were able to survive the initial exposures had this level of underlying genetic diversity and variants to offer a higher degree of fitness,” Breen added. “Obviously that’s speculation, and we don’t know exactly what’s happened. But it is fair to say that we used a very robust analysis and found signatures of selection in biologically relevant regions.”

Reference: “Evidence of Selective Response in the Free-Breeding Dog Population in Chornobyl” by Megan N. Dillon, Reade B. Roberts, Jennifer A. Betz, Timothy A. Mousseau, Norman J. Kleiman and Matthew Breen, 26 September 2026, Genes. DOI: 10.3390/genes17101195

#6501. Too Much Exercise Could Change Your Brain Chemistry in Unexpected Ways

Two days after an exercise test, mice subjected to weeks of grueling training still had elevated dopamine levels in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory and emotional regulation. The findings suggest that excessive exercise without adequate recovery can produce lasting changes in brain chemistry.

The study, published in the journal Neuroscience, was conducted by researchers in Brazil. Because dopamine helps regulate motivation and alertness, the results raise questions about whether similar disruptions could contribute to sleep problems, anxiety, and persistent fatigue in overtrained athletes. However, these possible effects have not been demonstrated in humans.

To investigate how different levels of physical exertion affect the brain, the researchers compared mice subjected to two exercise protocols. One group completed a single treadmill session until exhaustion. The other underwent eight weeks of progressively more demanding training designed to simulate the physical strain associated with overtraining syndrome.

During the final week, the heavily trained mice exercised twice daily, with just four hours between sessions. Researchers then examined the animals’ hippocampi, measuring dopamine, serotonin, and proteins involved in neurotransmitter production and regulation.

The mice that completed a single exhausting run showed a rise in dopamine shortly afterward. In contrast, the chronically trained animals had elevated dopamine levels even 48 hours after their performance test, during a period intended for recovery. Levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme essential for dopamine synthesis, also remained elevated.

Dopamine is involved in several functions, including motivation, reward processing, and wakefulness. Its presence is not inherently harmful, but changes in its regulation could affect brain activity during periods when the body would normally be recovering.

Interestingly, the researchers found no significant changes in serotonin levels. Serotonin has long been investigated as a possible contributor to exercise-related fatigue, but these results suggest that the neurochemical effects of excessive training cannot be explained by serotonin alone.

“Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain,” said Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study’s first author. He conducted the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP), with support from FAPESP.

Overtraining syndrome occurs when prolonged physical demands exceed the body’s ability to recover, potentially causing declining athletic performance, chronic fatigue, muscle pain, loss of appetite, increased injuries, and changes in immune and metabolic function. Researchers suspect that changes in brain signaling may also contribute to some symptoms.

Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, suggested that similar dopamine disturbances in humans might help explain connections between excessive training and sleep disorders. However, the researchers did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness in the mice, so the findings cannot establish a connection between the observed chemical changes and those symptoms.

The research team is now participating in an international project to identify which biological systems first begin to show abnormal responses when excessive exercise interferes with the body’s usual adaptations to training. Such work could help clarify how beneficial physical activity progresses into a state of insufficient recovery and impaired performance.

Reference: “Excessive training alters hippocampal tyrosine hydroxylase and dopamine homeostasis in mice” by Alisson Luiz da Rocha, João Pedro Floriano, Ana Paula Pinto, Dennys Esper Cintra, Eduardo Rochete Ropelle, Ellen Cristini de Freitas, José Rodrigo Pauli and Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, 4 August 2026, Neuroscience. DOI: 10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.08.006

A new study revealed that people who rely on AI for basic tasks become less motivated over time. Live Science polled its readers on whether they have experienced this situation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While people use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to help with tasks like learning new skills or answering questions, a new study suggests that these benefits may come with a downside.

The findings, presented at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco earlier this month, revealed that people who used AI assistance for reading comprehension or math problems were more likely to struggle or give up when the AI assistance was removed. The results suggest that relying too much on AI could lower people's motivations to overcome challenging situations.

In the wake of this study, Live Science recently polled its readers on whether they felt AI was making them less motivated after using it.

More than 140 readers voted in the poll, with 30% of voters picking "No, I don't use AI at all, so this situation doesn't apply to me."

"If AI were only a tool, controlled by those who use it I might give it a try," said one commenter in response. "But it isn't under control at all. It gets into your bank accounts and moves money without authorization. It encourages suicide and self-harm. It is addictive and makes people lazy. I know someone who uses it to answer questions and while it is detailed, it makes her lazier, asking one question and getting the answer without her searching for it. AI Is a danger. It should not be allowed."

Other comments reflected this sentiment, with one reader writing, "Use of all automatic aids decrease[s] attention and retention. I see it in the use of navigation devices where drivers ought to recognize routes after a couple of times. AI helps research and cuts down lengthy searches, but over use of summaries weakens critical faculties."

Other commenters questioned whether AI is the problem, or if people are just inclined to take the easy option, asking "Would you get the same results if the answers to all but a few problems were provided on separate sheet of paper?" and another writing, "I think researchers should also investigate whether shovels decrease motivation to dig holes with one's hands. AI, like a shovel, is only a tool."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know in the comments!

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027.
