#6466. Comets Probably Didn’t Bring Life’s Ingredients to Earth After All, New Study Reveals

New research suggests Mars may have been better suited than Earth to receive life’s chemical ingredients from comets, although the chances remain surprisingly slim.

Comets have long been considered possible sources of the chemical ingredients that helped life emerge on Earth. But new research suggests these icy visitors were extremely unlikely to deliver those molecules in sufficient quantities, challenging a theory that has shaped scientific thinking for nearly a century.

Using advanced computer simulations, researchers led by the University of Cambridge found that comet impacts would almost always destroy fragile organic compounds before they could contribute to the chemistry of early life. Even under favorable conditions, successful delivery would have been extraordinarily rare. The findings, published in Scientific Reports, also suggest that Mars may have offered slightly better conditions for receiving these molecules.

Comets contain carbon and nitrogen-bearing compounds, including hydrogen cyanide (HCN), a molecule involved in chemical reactions that can produce some of life’s essential building blocks. Their ability to transport these substances across the Solar System has made them central to theories about how prebiotic chemistry began on Earth.

“Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a ‘get out of jail free card’ that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life,” said lead author Dr. Richard Anslow from Cambridge’s Institute of Astronomy. “It’s kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it’s highly unlikely.”

The problem lies in the violence of comet impacts. According to the simulations, comets generally approach Earth at speeds and angles that make the survival of their organic cargo extremely unlikely. Most of these molecules would vaporize during impact rather than reach the surface intact. The researchers reached this conclusion by combining models of comet trajectories, atmospheric interactions, impact physics, and the formation and evolution of comet populations.

To investigate the likelihood of successful delivery, the team concentrated on HCN, which is regularly detected in Solar System comets. Their calculations showed that impacts capable of preserving the molecule and depositing it at useful concentrations would have been exceptionally uncommon.

The number of comets striking Earth also fell sharply during the planet’s first 500 million years, leaving at most a handful of opportunities for meaningful HCN delivery. Even if some molecules survived, they would likely disperse before the chemical reactions needed for life’s emergence could advance far enough.

“It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going,” said Anslow. “We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way. But it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke.”

The investigation builds on earlier research published in 2023, when Anslow and several colleagues proposed that closely spaced planets could help comets deliver organic molecules. In such systems, gravitational encounters might allow comets to move between planets while gradually slowing down, increasing the chances that their chemical cargo could survive an eventual impact.

The new study examined whether similar conditions could have existed in our Solar System, using recent advances in simulations of comet impacts and planetary dynamics.

“We’re learning more and more all the time about how our Solar System and the Earth formed, and pulling this together with lots of different advances in modeling, which allowed us to investigate this idea that has been around for close to a century,” Anslow said.

If comets were not a major source of Earth’s prebiotic molecules, other explanations remain possible. Asteroids struck the early Earth much more frequently, and their impacts could have triggered chemical reactions that produced organic compounds. Alternatively, the necessary ingredients may have formed through chemical processes occurring on Earth itself, without requiring delivery from space.

Although the results cast doubt on cometary delivery to Earth, the researchers identified Mars as a somewhat more favorable destination. Mars is smaller than Earth and currently has a much thinner atmosphere, conditions that could allow more cometary material to reach its surface. This may have increased the chances of organic molecules surviving impacts during the Solar System’s early history, when comet collisions were more common.

However, the simulations do not establish that comets successfully delivered prebiotic molecules to Mars. They indicate only that the process may have been more feasible there than on Earth.

“This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars,” said Anslow. “Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative, is that it didn’t happen on either planet.”

The findings could also help astronomers assess the chemical environments of planets orbiting other stars. In planetary systems where several worlds orbit close together, gravitational interactions might slow incoming comets enough to improve the prospects for delivering organic molecules.

Future observatories, including proposed successors to the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory, could help investigate these planetary systems. Identifying environments where “bouncing” comets might survive long enough to deliver their chemical cargo could provide one way to narrow the search for potentially habitable worlds.

Reference: “Cometary impacts an unlikely pathway towards the origins of life on Earth” by Richard J. Anslow, Catriona H. McDonald, Amy Bonsor, Paul B. Rimmer and Auriol S. P. Rae, 28 October 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-74214-y

The research was supported in part by the Royal Society, the Leverhulme Centre for Life in the Universe, and the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI).

In his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats," biologist James O'Hanlon surveys deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it adds up to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most trickery in nature happens without a shred of awareness behind it. An orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) doesn't know it looks like a flower, and a moth with eyespots on its wings has no concept of the predator it's startling. These are adaptations shaped by natural selection over countless generations, not conscious choices. But a smaller set of animal behaviors look like something else entirely — deliberate tactical, and aimed at manipulating another individual's beliefs, the same way human lies do.

Figuring out which is which turns out to be one of the trickiest questions in animal behavior research, James O'Hanlon, zoologist and science communicator, told Live Science.

In this excerpt from his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), O'Hanlon explores camouflage, mimicry and misdirection throughout the natural world, building toward the book's central question: Can animals tell lies?

In it, O'Hanlon examines one of the strongest candidates for an animal that deliberately lies: the fork-tailed drongo (Dicrurus adsimilis), a small African bird whose ever-changing repertoire of false alarm calls has made it a favorite subject for scientists studying tactical deception.

James O'Hanlon interview: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're publishing for free to all our readers. If you'd like more exclusive book excerpts, as well as news analysis, scientist interviews and in-depth features, please consider subscribing.

Fork-tailed drongos are remarkable vocal mimics and can do an uncanny impression of a meerkat alarm call. The meerkats respond to it just as they would one of their own and scamper to safety. Meanwhile the drongo flies in once more to steal the meerkats' abandoned food.

They don't stop there; drongos mimic a whole range of other animals' signals, mimicking various avian neighbors like the caped glossy starling or the pied babbler. Those ever-watchful meerkats fall for the ruse once more, leaving their meals behind. Researchers have identified over fifty unique deceptive vocalizations in the drongo's arsenal.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By constantly rotating their "cry-wolf" tactics, these birds ensure their victims don't grow wise to the deception, allowing the theft to continue unabated. Yet, their cleverness isn't reserved solely for exploited meerkats.

This remarkable talent for mimicry extends to other creatures as well. Pied babblers and sociable weavers, who both forage in groups upon the earth, frequently find themselves bamboozled into fleeing their food by these false warnings. Had the legendary boy who cried wolf possessed such adaptive ingenuity, he might have successfully maintained his trickery.

It would, however, have resulted in a peculiar fable with an entirely different, perhaps darker, moral lesson.

It's early days in our understanding of whether animals can tell lies. Social group-living animals are likely candidates for finding animal tricksters in the wild, and we have only scratched the surface of what kinds of trickery goes on in these societies. Time will tell whether similar forms of deception are happening in the subsonic songs of whales and dolphins, the chemical mists of ants and termites, or the barks and howls of wild dogs.

Meerkats are tricked by fork-tailed drongos mimicking the alarm calls, so the birds can swoop in and steal their food.

Despite the growing list of evidence, scientists are still hesitant to conclude definitively that animals can intentionally deceive another, in a similar way to humans. This might have more to do with the professional conduct of scientists than it has to do with the reality of what goes on in animal societies.

Firstly, one of the most important rules in studying animal behaviour is to not anthropomorphise animals. In other words, don't project human-like qualities or emotions onto other species. Scientists must be completely objective and not assume that other animals think, behave or make decisions for the same reasons we do.

Since lying has always been perceived as a human behaviour, scientists are incredibly hesitant to conclude that it could be happening in other animals.

The second reason is that scientists are trained to never definitively conclude anything. There is an idea in science that you can disprove things, but never really prove things. This is why you will find scientific writing littered with phrases like "the evidence suggests," "it's probable that," or — my personal favourite — "the most parsimonious explanation is," and so on and so forth.

A professional scientist will often give a direct "No" answer but rarely a direct "Yes." It's like squeezing blood from a stone. But this is a good thing. What often sounds like indecisiveness or a lack of certainty is actually just good professional practice. It's part of a scientist's job description — to consider all possible explanations for the observations they have made and examine every possibility on its own merits.

Then the conclusions that are drawn come down to which of these possibilities is most likely. In a universe of infinite possibilities and scales of enquiry, it would take an impossible amount of overwhelming data for scientists to exclude all possibilities but one.

#6463. Three-quarters of NFL football players may end up with CTE

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

It’s the first population-level estimate for the neurogenerative disease among NFL players

The neurodegenerative disease CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy. The condition has been identified most frequently among American football players.

An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.

Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.

A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.

The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.

The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.

#6462. 120 Million Years Ago, Something Extraordinary Was Happening in Earth’s Oceans

Colombia’s ancient seas supported an extraordinary diversity of top predators, offering clues to how life may undergo major evolutionary changes without a mass extinction.

Mass extinctions have reshaped life on Earth, but they may not be the only way ecosystems undergo dramatic evolutionary change.

Roughly 120 million years ago, the seas covering what is now central Colombia were home to an extraordinary mix of ancient Jurassic survivors and emerging Cretaceous predators. Fossils from this remarkably complex ecosystem suggest that some of evolution’s biggest turning points may unfold without a catastrophic mass extinction.

The evidence comes from the Early Cretaceous Paja Formation near Villa de Leyva, Colombia, where the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) houses most of the formation’s fossils. The research at McGill University and CIP was conducted by PhD graduate Dirley Cortés and Professor Hans Larsson of McGill’s Department of Biology.

“This geological formation has produced an exceptionally rich fossil record that includes giant marine reptiles like long-necked plesiosaurs and marine crocodile relatives, as well as turtles, sharks, crustaceans and others,” Cortés explained. “Together, these animals formed the Paja Biota, one of the most ecologically complex marine communities found to date.”

In a previous study, the researchers estimated the Paja Biota’s food web, the network of feeding relationships among its animals. They found it was among the most complex ever to have evolved, with a high diversity of apex predators, animals at the top of the food chain.

“The Paja Formation records an extraordinary process in the history of life, when a ‘perfect storm’ of environmental factors we know to promote ecological complexity coincided with ancient lineages that were about to disappear. At the same time, new groups were beginning to flourish,” Larsson said.

The researchers suspect that greenhouse temperatures, high sea levels, and nutrient-rich coastal waters helped support this exceptional biodiversity and biological transition. New marine connections between the eastern Pacific and early Atlantic oceans through what is now Colombia were probably also part of that rare convergence. Many of these same factors help drive biodiversity today, they noted.

Cortés and Larsson propose calling the pattern a “Biotic Inflection,” a period when many evolutionary lineages nearing extinction coexist with newly emerging groups that later diversify.

“I think we’ve discovered a new model of global biodiversity change. Now we’ll need to see just how widespread this could be in Earth’s history and how we can quantify its impacts,” Larsson said.

Testing the proposal will require additional fossil sampling, more precise dating, and comparisons with deposits elsewhere in the world. Those investigations would help establish how widespread the Biotic Inflection pattern was and when similar events may have occurred in Earth’s history.

Reference: “The Paja Formation of Colombia records uniquely high biodiversity during a biotic inflection in an Early Cretaceous Gondwanan marine ecosystem” by Dirley Cortés and Hans C. E. Larsson, 15 May 2026, Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution. DOI: 10.3389/fevo.2026.1848892

#6461. Trapped in Amber for 99 Million Years, a Lizard’s Tail Reveals an Ancient Survival Secret

A clean break in 99-million-year-old amber offers rare direct evidence that ancient lizards shed their tails using a defensive mechanism still common today.

A lizard can escape a predator by leaving its tail behind, sometimes with the detached piece still wriggling as the animal makes its getaway. It’s a remarkable defense, but scientists have struggled to determine how far back it goes. Ancient reptile fossils can show where a tail was capable of breaking, yet that doesn’t necessarily mean the animal could shed it to escape danger.

An unusually revealing clue has now emerged from a tiny piece of amber discovered in northern Myanmar. Measuring just 18 millimeters (about 0.7 inches) long, the amber holds a lizard’s tail that detached approximately 99 million years ago. What makes it so valuable is the remarkably preserved point where the tail separated from the body. Researchers say it provides the best-preserved direct fossil evidence of autotomy, the defensive mechanism that allows lizards to shed their tails.

For years, no one recognized what was trapped inside the amber. Dolev Fabrikant, a PhD candidate at Tel Aviv University’s New Environmental School, was examining what appeared to be a tiny twig or fragment of an insect when he noticed something unusual about its surface. “I realized that what seemed to be a twig was covered in tiny scales,” he recalls. “It was a lizard’s tail.”

Fabrikant shared his discovery with his supervisor, Dr. Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou of Tel Aviv University’s School of Zoology and Steinhardt Museum of Natural History, whose reaction was immediate.

“I nearly jumped out of my chair,” says Dr. Davranoglou. “I instantly realized that this tiny fossil could open an extraordinary window into the past, helping us understand the history of one of the most widespread survival strategies among reptiles. Until now, we could only speculate on whether ancient lizards could shed their tails. We now have direct evidence that one could.”

Getting a closer look at the fossil was another challenge. The amber was cloudy, and the structures inside were too small for an ordinary microscope to reveal the details researchers needed. Rather than cutting open the specimen, the team turned to micro-CT scanning at Israel’s Volcani Institute.

“Micro-CT takes X-ray images from many angles and combines them into a three-dimensional reconstruction. It allowed us to examine structures hidden by the amber without needing to cut this one-of-a-kind piece open,” explains Dr. Ahmed Nasser, Head of the institute’s Inter-Institutional Analytical Unit.

At the severed end of the tail, the scans revealed a distinctive ring of tissue closely resembling the structure found in tails shed by living lizards. The separation itself was relatively clean and symmetrical, without the damage patterns that would be expected if the tail had broken off in an accident.

That distinction matters because other reptile fossils have offered less conclusive evidence. Some preserve natural fracture planes in the tail vertebrae, while others contain regenerated tails, indicating that the animals had lost part of their tails previously. Although these features suggest that ancient reptiles possessed the ability to shed their tails, the presence of fracture planes alone cannot establish that they actually used this defense. In the Myanmar specimen, the preserved tissue and clean separation provide much stronger evidence that the tail was released through autotomy.

The researchers still cannot determine exactly what kind of lizard left the tail behind. Without the rest of its skeleton, including the skull, there are too few anatomical clues to identify its closest relatives.

“Although we can securely identify this specimen as a lizard, we lack the skull and other skeletal features that would allow a more secure identification. Possible affinities include the groups containing today’s wall lizards or, alternatively, slow worms and monitor lizards,” says Apostolos Christopoulos, a PhD candidate at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens.

How the tail ended up in amber is another mystery. The lizard might have become stuck in sticky resin and shed its tail to free itself. It is also possible that a predator attacked the animal, prompting it to release its tail, which later landed in resin.

Reference: “Direct fossil evidence of caudal autotomy in a Cretaceous lizard” by Dolev Fabrikant, Apostolos Christopoulos, Ahmed Nasser and Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou, October 2026, Palaeontologia Electronica. DOI: 10.26879/1706

#6456. A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud might not need dust to kick-start its formation

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud emerges every day during spring and summer on Mars, a long wispy ribbon downwind of the Arsia Mons volcano. This image of the cloud was captured by a camera aboard the European Space Agency’s Mars Express mission.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.

The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.

Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.

There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.

Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.

The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.

The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.

While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.

The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.

“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.

Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

D.E. Siskind et al. Understanding the effects of polar mesospheric clouds on the environment of the upper mesosphere and lower thermosphere. Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres. 2018. doi: 10.1029/2018JD028830

B.J. Murray and E.J. Jensen. Homogeneous nucleation of amorphous solid water particles in the upper mesosphere. Journal of Atmospheric and Solar-Terrestrial Physics. 2010. doi: 10.1016/j.jastp.2009.10.007

Archaeologists have unearthed a human-shaped funeral offering that may represent an ancient Japanese priestess.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have discovered a ghostly human-shaped artifact at a fifth-century burial mound in Japan. The clay figurine's appearance suggests it represents a female shaman who once guarded a tomb.

The artifact was unearthed at the archaeological site of Nishikaminomiya, northwest of Tokyo, according to a translated statement from Japan's Gunma prefectural government. At the site, archaeologists found nearly a dozen burial mounds known as "kofun" dated to the fifth and sixth centuries.

This time period in Japanese history, which lasted from about A.D. 300 to 710, is called the Kofun period. Many tombs in this period had cylindrical clay sculptures called "haniwa" that were used as offerings to the dead and were often thought to contain the souls of the deceased.

The newly unearthed haniwa is about 16 inches (40 centimeters) tall; but only the head and torso remain, so it would have originally been a lot larger. The figurine was discovered in a moat around an enormous burial mound that measured about 145 feet (45 meters) in diameter. It's likely that the haniwa was originally placed near a boat-shaped sarcophagus archaeologists discovered in the mound and that it slipped down the hill over time to land in the moat, according to the statement.

An aerial view of the tomb where archaeologists found the shrine maiden statuette.

Experts think the haniwa represents a female shaman known as a "miko," or "shrine maiden." These priestesses bridge the gap between the human and spiritual realms in the Shinto religion. During the Kofun period, miko would have performed important funeral rituals and offered spiritual guidance.

The haniwa figurine has a traditional Japanese topknot hairstyle called a "shimada," which indicates that the haniwa represents a miko, according to the statement. Both of the figurine's wrists have bracelets made from clay and red pigment. The haniwa's fingers have been carefully molded, and the figurine has a prominent nose. In addition, she wears a red sash painted on her torso and holds a rod-shaped ritual implement in her left hand.

"These details suggest that considerable care was taken in making the figure, even in features that would not be visible from a distance," representatives of the Gunma prefectural government said in the statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Archaeologists discovered the haniwa this year during excavations of the main burial mound at Nishikaminomiya, but they have been working at the site since 2020.

The haniwa is currently on display at the Gunma Prefectural Archaeological Research Center's Excavation Information Museum in the city of Shibukawa.

#6452. Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Madagascan flying foxes, easy targets for hunters, have shrunk since the 1980s

Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) (shown) have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. Large-scale hunting by humans may be the reason.

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).

“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.

As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

How did the universe transition from an impenetrable fog of hydrogen into the bright and starlit cosmos we see today? Astronomers think they're onto the answer.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The mysterious force that cleared the cosmic fog at the dawn of the universe may not be what we thought, a new study suggests. The results hint that astronomers may need to rethink a major aspect of cosmological evolution, which led to the universe we clearly see today.

Around 400,000 years after the Big Bang, the fledgling universe finally cooled enough to form atoms — mostly hydrogen. But these neutral, non-electrically charged hydrogen atoms shrouded the cosmos in a fog that made it opaque to ultraviolet (UV) light.

Then, after the first stars flickered to life and gathered into galaxies, bursts of radiation ionized the neutral hydrogen. This turned the impenetrable fog of atoms into electrically charged protons and electrons, allowing light to pass through interstellar space unimpeded and, eventually, reach our observatories. This cosmic curtain parting is known as the Epoch of Reionization, or what a team of researchers studying it call the "last major phase transition in the universe."

A chart showing the evolution of the universe, from the Big Bang to today. The first stars started to appear from the hydrogen fog a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," Cody Carr, an astronomer who focuses on galaxy evolution at the University of Michigan and first author of a new study of the epoch, said in a statement. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."

Astrophysicists previously thought that this fog-clearing effect depended on supernovas, the violently explosive deaths of stars around eight to 50 times the mass of the sun.

But in the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Astronomy, Carr and colleagues presented evidence that supernovas exerted the opposite effect, trapping the so-called Lyman continuum (LyC) photons of ionizing UV radiation that dispelled the celestial fog instead of scattering them.

"The most interesting thing about our paper is the observation that the strongest LyC emitters do not have fast galactic winds," Carr told Live Science via email. "This challenges the notion that galaxies require fast supernova-driven winds to enable LyC escape."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers used the Hubble Space Telescope to observe an analogue of the ancient universe in the local cosmos: six star-forming, wind-launching galaxies around 3.5 billion light-years away.

These compact starburst galaxies are generally smaller than 6,500 light-years in diameter and form around 10 solar masses' worth of stars per year. That star-birthing rate is several times higher than that of the Milky Way, which is up to 20 times larger.

The galaxies' spectra, or light-based fingerprints, revealed the origin, chemical composition, speed and direction of their stellar winds, which were whipped up by the radiation from their newly formed stars.

The researchers also described how these processes changed as the massive young stars evolved and died in energetic supernovas several billion years later, with the resultant galactic winds overpowering the stellar winds.

These nearby galaxies highlighted a counterintuitive two-phase process.

In the initial phase, which occurred during the first 3 million years of star formation, the newly formed massive stars' stellar winds carved through their galaxies' neutral gas and dust at nearly 2,000 miles per second (3,000 kilometers per second). This allowed LyC light to escape the galaxy and ionize the neutral gas and dust in intergalactic space.

The second phase, which emerged around 3 million years after star formation, seemed to reverse this process. As O-type stars — the hottest, bluest and most massive stars in the cosmos — lived fast and died young, their expelled stellar guts added to the opaque galactic gas and dust, churning it and loading it with mass, which created a trap for LyC light.

The oldest galaxies in this study ‪—‬ and, therefore, the ones with the fastest supernova-generated galactic winds ‪—‬ allowed the least amount of ionizing radiation to escape their environs.

"In general, our results are in disagreement with most cosmological simulations, which typically show the LyC escape fraction peaking after the launch of supernova-driven winds," Carr explained via email. In other words, supernovas didn't drive the Epoch of Reionization, but they may have dampened it. The intense light of newborn stars now seems like the most viable source of reionization.

Future research could aim to obtain additional galactic samples and higher-resolution observations across other wavelengths.

Carr, C., Cen, R., McCandliss, S., Ford, J., Saldana-Lopez, A., Scarlata, C., Huberty, M. S., Jaskot, A., Flury, S., Oey, M. S., Amorín, R. O., Borthakur, S., Haye, M., Heckman, T., Ji, Z., Komarova, L., Reste, A. L., Leclercq, F., Marques-Chaves, R., . . . Xu, X. (2026). Lyman continuum escape during the onset of galactic winds in compact starbursts. Nature Astronomy. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02999-z

#6447. Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Fast east-west flights unlink birds’ internal clocks from the sun, scrambling navigation

A Manx shearwater soars in midflight. New research suggests that a phenomenon akin to jet lag can disrupt the seabirds’ ability to navigate using the sun.

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.

“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

Each of Earth's hemispheres experiences summer, but how do they differ?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Each year, Earth's Northern and Southern hemispheres cycle through four seasons, including summer.

Given that the hemispheres are symmetric about the equator, you may think that, on both sides of the world, summers should be similar – both in terms of their climate and factors like their length. But are Northern and Southern hemisphere summers really the same?

Climate experts tell Live Science that they differ quite a bit — and that comes with a clear recommendation for sun enthusiasts.

The most obvious difference is that Northern and Southern summers happen at different times. According to NASA, this arises because Earth's axis is tilted 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of our planet's orbit around the sun.

This tilt causes the Northern and Southern hemispheres to be oriented toward the sun at different times throughout the year. Between the Northern Hemisphere's summer solstice and autumnal equinox, the Northern Hemisphere is oriented toward the sun, resulting in summer, and vice versa in the Southern Hemisphere.

This means that summers between the Northern and Southern hemispheres sit six months out of sync with each other — with Northern summers spanning late June to late September and Southern ones going from late December to late March. (Summers are also defined meteorologically, or relative to changes in weather phenomena, as being the hottest months of the year. Under this definition, Northern summers run from June to August, and Southern ones go from December to February.)

Another difference between Northern and Southern summers is their duration. According to NASA, Northern Hemisphere summers are, on average, 4.5 days longer than Southern Hemisphere summers. (This is with respect to the astronomical definition; meteorologically, Northern summers are longer than Southern ones by two days in non-leap years, but this is due to February being the calendar's shortest month.)

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The 4.5-day difference occurs because Earth's orbit around the sun is slightly elliptical instead of perfectly circular, according to NASA. Consequently, Earth's orbital velocity (the speed at which our planet hurtles around the sun) isn't constant.

Earth isn't the only planet that experiences such a dichotomy in the duration of seasons. According to NASA, Mars does too: Northern summers on the Red Planet are 24 Martian days — 24.66 Earth days — longer than the planet's Southern Hemisphere's summers. This greater difference is because Mars's orbit is much more oval-shaped than Earth's.

During the Northern Hemisphere's summer, Earth is farther away from the sun and thus moving more slowly, said Georg Feulner, a senior researcher at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany. This is due to Kepler's second law of planetary motion, he added.

This means that at aphelion ‪(the point at which our planet is farthest from the sun)‬ Earth is traveling at 18.2 miles per second (29.3 kilometers per second). This jumps to 18.82 miles per second (30.29 km/s) at perihelion ‪(the point when Earth is closest to the sun ) which occurs during Southern summers.

While this may seem like a tiny difference in speed, it causes our planet's path around the sun to be 53,686 miles (86,400 kilometers) shorter in a 24-hour-interval at aphelion compared with at perihelion. In other words, Earth covers more "ground" at aphelion than at perihelion over a 24-hour-interval. "Therefore, the time between the Northern Hemisphere spring and autumn equinoxes is longer than the time between the Southern Hemisphere spring and autumn equinoxes, Feulner told Live Science in an email.

A third point of difference is that Northern summers are typically hotter than Southern ones. A 2015 study in the journal Climate Dynamics showed the precise value of this depends on whether temperatures are measured on the surface air, land or ocean, and the latitude at which they're taken. Nonetheless, when averaged over all domains and latitudes, Northern summers are 7.83 degrees Fahrenheit (4.35 degrees Celsius) hotter than Southern ones.

So what's behind this? Earth's changing distance from the sun isn't important. If it were, Earth's aphelion crossing during Northern summers should make them cooler than Southern summers during the perihelion crossing. Instead, several other factors are responsible.

One is the Northern Hemisphere's bigger fraction of land compared to its large water bodies like oceans. "Land has a lower heat capacity than water and so increases temperature more for a given heating than water does," Richard Seager, a professor at Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, told Live Science in an email. As a result, the many inland sites in the Northern Hemisphere heat up rapidly and have higher summer temperatures, according to the UCAR Center for Science Education.

Additionally, Seager said, another difference lies in the way heat is distributed through air and water. The solar heat that land receives warms only the first few feet of the atmosphere, while the heat water absorbs gets mixed throughout its depths. This makes the Southern Hemisphere — with its larger fraction of water — cooler over summer.

The second factor for the North Hemisphere's higher summer temperatures are cross-equatorial ocean currents. Such currents cross the equator, transferring water and heat between the hemispheres. The primary current is the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Current (AMOC). "The AMOC transports heat from the SH [Southern Hemisphere] to the NH in the Atlantic," Feulner said. This warms Northern oceans and seas, which, in turn, heats up adjacent land-masses.

So, Northern Hemisphere summers are longer and hotter than Southern ones. If you want to stretch out your summer, you now know where to go.

The Cat's Head Nebula shows its ghostly insides and sinister red eye in rival views from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In space, nobody can hear you scream — or meow, for that matter. This was as true for Félicette — the stray Parisian tuxedo cat who safely completed the world's first (and only) suborbital feline flight, in 1963 — as it is for the gargantuan Cat's Head Nebula, which is featured in stunning new images from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

Rising from the cloudy Carina Nebula some 7,500 light-years from Earth, the Cat's Head Nebula is a column of star-sculpted gas and dust that vaguely resembles a feline sitting with its back to us, coyly turning its head to show off a single red eye. That eye is a young star that's embedded deep within the dust and possibly transforming it before our eyes.

Nebulas like these occur when the radiation from active young stars lights up and erodes the material around them. They are beautiful and easy to find; if this cosmic cat gets bored staring at us, it can just waltz over to the other side of the Carina Nebula and crawl into a similar globule of gas that looks exactly like a box with an open lid. (Cats will be cats, after all.)

In honor of Halloween, the European Space Agency (ESA) shared three competing views of the Cat's Head Nebula — one from the Hubble Space Telescope, which captures optical light, and two from the infrared instruments aboard the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The three views, shown below, reveal different features of the nebula in different wavelengths of light, getting progressively spookier as more color drains out of the scene.Take a look at all three images — and cast your vote for the spookiest in the poll at the end.

The Hubble Space Telescope's optical light view of the Cat's Head Nebula.

Observing the nebula in the same visible wavelength range that you could see through a strong backyard telescope, Hubble highlights the dark pillar of dust that has survived the ultraviolet assault of nearby stars. The wispy edges at the right of the column show where starlight is evaporating the gas around it, slowly whittling it away to nothing.

The glow of blue, yellow, orange and red light around the dust pillar mark where starlight is interacting with different gas molecules, including oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur, according to ESA. The process is similar to how different molecules in Earth's atmosphere produce different-colored auroras when excited by solar radiation — just on a much grander scale.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in near-infrared light.

Switching to light human eyes cannot see, JWST's Near-Infrared Camera cuts through the wispier outer layers of dust to show the densest material at the column's center. Countless additional stars and galaxies appear in the field of view as their infrared glow penetrates the surrounding material.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Here we see a more complex, turbulent column, showing how stellar radiation is carving up the inside of the cat's head as well as its edges. JWST's view also illuminates a disembodied, hand-like structure to the left of the cat, reaching out as if to pet its cosmic companion.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in mid-infrared light.

The final view, taken with JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, cuts to the ghostly core of the nebula, showing little more than smoky, bluish light. According to ESA, these are the emissions of molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — typically colorless molecules of carbon and hydrogen related to combustion.

While most starlight disappears in this view, a strange new bright spot emerges to the right of the cat's head. This orange speck is a true mystery, according to ESA, and its relationship to the rest of the nebula is unknown.

#6442. Your Genes May Already Know Who You’ll Fall in Love With

Observable traits often determined by genetics may attract us to someone who shares them.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Besides the clichéd “must love dogs” and “likes long walks on the beach at sunset,” what do people actually look for when seeking a partner? Dating profiles barely touch on the qualities someone might imagine in their ideal match, and bathroom selfies aren’t doing us any favors. Sometimes the answer is so subconscious, it can only be found in our genes.

Trying to find the person who’s right for us is less random than we might think. When individuals with similar traits find each other, it’s known as assortative mating, which continues shaping the genetic makeup of human populations and is intentional—in a way—whether those couples realize it or not. In the back of our minds are criteria, such as education or certain behaviors, that potential matches have to meet. This can partly explain why some families have been known for certain traits for generations. Researcher Gretchen Saunders of the University of Minnesota decided to find out just how prevalent this phenomenon is by comparing genetic signatures in couples and across generations.

“Understanding mate choice, including how it is changing over time, is critical for both social science and genetics research, as it informs patterns of social homogamy and inequality while also affecting key assumptions in quantitative genetic and genetic epidemiological models,” Saunders, who specializes in statistical genetics and psychology, said in a study recently published in Behavior Genetics.

When partners carry similar traits that can be inherited, their children are also highly likely to be born with them, which can affect how those traits end up being distributed throughout a population. This doesn’t necessarily mean people explicitly choose each other based on those traits alone. It’s more likely that they already associate with groups that share the traits, and through those social and professional connections, they may eventually find a partner in such a group. Saunders based her research on eight specific traits ranging from physical features to education to habits that affect health. These included the visible factors of height and body mass index along with education level. She added five more having to do with drinking and smoking, such as frequency and the start or end of these habits.

Each subject who provided information for the study was given a polygenic score. These are numbers that merge the effects of different DNA variants in the genome to gauge a person’s genetic predisposition to a phenotypic, or observable, trait. Polygenic scores can also predict the likelihood of inherited diseases, which was not a factor in Saunders’ research. She was especially looking for similarities in polygenic scores between spouses and siblings. The phenotypic factor that was most similar between married couples was education level, which wasn’t surprising given that sociocultural variables have been observed in couples with phenotypic similarities for decades. Education was followed closely by alcoholic drinks per week. Less obvious links were body mass index, smoking initiation, and smoking cessation.

Seemingly unrelated traits were often found together. Those who had completed a higher level of education were often found to prefer partners who were taller, had a lower body mass index, and lower likelihood of smoking. Heavy smokers and drinkers tended to be attracted to those with similar habits and a higher body mass index. Polygenic scores based on this data revealed that while spousal genetic correlations were not as strong, they were still substantial. Traits already determined before these subjects became couples, such as height and body mass index, were the most correlated, while traits that were subject to change over time, such as cigarettes or drinks per day and smoking cessation, showed less of a connection. Comparing siblings showed evidence for partner matching based on these traits in earlier generations.

“Apparent differences in genetic architecture across cohorts may reflect not only temporal changes in assortative mating within populations, but also cross-cohort differences in underlying social structure, opportunity, and behavioral norms that shape mating patterns and phenotype distributions,” Saunders said.

So while DNA isn’t necessarily destiny, it may be, at the very least, pointing you in the right direction.

#6441. A proof-of-concept test can spot bladder cancer in urine

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Urine may also reveal the presence of kidney and prostrate cancers

A new proof-of-concept test surveys RNA in urine to spot bladder cancer. RNA carries information that can reveal what cancer is present and how it is behaving.

Andrew Brookes/Connect Images/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A splash of pee could reveal bladder cancer.

Using a proof-of-concept urine test that decodes RNA molecules, it’s possible to pick out patients with the disease, scientists report October 2 in Nature Medicine. Because urine is in direct contact with bladder tumors, it’s “a very attractive fluid” to look for this type of cancer, says Stanford University oncologist Maximilian Diehn. The technology, still in its infancy, offers a glimpse of what future screening tests might entail.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Today’s liquid biopsies for cancer, which examine bodily fluids rather than tissue samples, largely focus on finding DNA that tumors shed into the blood. Diehn’s lab sought a different stream of information. The researchers analyzed RNA, DNA’s molecular cousin. RNA isn’t as stable as DNA, so it hasn’t been researchers’ top target. But it carries info that DNA lacks, such as which genes are turned on. That’s important, Diehn says, “because it can tell you what the cancer is doing at any given moment.”

Diehn and his colleagues previously developed a technique to analyze dribs of RNA floating in blood. In samples from people with lung cancer, the team could read RNA signatures of the disease. Now, the researchers have shown that their technique is a whiz at detecting cancer in urine. The team tested their technique using samples from 515 cancer patients and healthy people. It was sensitive enough to identify 95 out of 100 people with bladder cancer — even at early stages of disease. What’s more, the test also offered hints about cancer biology, such as the type of tumor and risk of recurrence. Those details could help doctors make decisions about treatments, Diehn says.

The researchers are now exploring their technique’s potential for picking up other cancers. Their evidence suggests that it can spot cancer in the kidney and prostate, organs also washed by urine. One day, Diehn says, he can imagine a multi-cancer urine test focused on tumors in the genitourinary tract. But there’s much to do before such a test makes it into clinics.

Because the technology is so new, the jury’s still out on whether RNA-based testing will find use in cancer screening, Diehn says. “But absolutely, I think the field needs to investigate it.”

#6440. A Startup Wants to Put 50,000 Mirrors in Space. The Goal: Make Sunlight Available at Night.

For $5,000 an hour, Reflect Orbital will bring you the power of the sun no matter what time of night it is. Astronomers are sounding the alarm.

With the launch of Sputnik in October 1957, humanity officially entered the satellite era, and in the ensuing decades, the thousands of satellites sent into space have drastically changed life on the ground. These sprawling networks of orbital spacecraft provide us with constant GPS navigation, communication, weather forecasting, and an unprecedented level of scientific surveys. But for ground-based astronomers, satellites have been a steadily growing headache.

Problems really started back in 2019 when SpaceX launched the first cadre of Starlink satellites, and almost immediately their immense number and brightness disrupted ground-based observations of space. Today, there are more than 11,000 Starlink satellites, and scientists worry about their impact on next-generation telescopes, including the new Vera Rubin Observatory in Chile.

Now astronomers may have an even bigger problem on their hands: Reflect Orbital. If you haven’t heard of this company, that’s not surprising. Unlike SpaceX, they currently don’t have any satellites in orbit at all, but what they plan to do with those satellites once they’re nestled within Earth’s orbit has astrophysicists begging for the federal government to intervene.

“This is not a ‘concern’—this is like a bullet in your head,” Princeton University astrophysicist Gaspar Bakos told Sky & Telescope. “It’s the end of ground-based astronomy.”

So what exactly has astronomers like Bakos up in arms? Well, Reflect Orbital bills itself as a “sunlight-as-a-service” company whose constellation of 50,000 satellites, each armed with massive mirrors, directs sunlight toward dark areas of the planet. The company says users could conceivably call for sunlight on demand to power solar panels or aid in nighttime search-and-rescue operations. But this altruistic vision likely obscures more lucrative use-cases for the military. That seems especially likely given the going rate for sunlight: $5,000 an hour, according to Sky & Telescope. That price is well beyond the budget of most search-and-rescue groups.

Then there’s life on the ground. Plants and animals, humans included, depend on a day-night cycle that’s existed since Earth formed in the fiery cauldron of our star’s protoplanetary disk. Artificial sunlight could throw that rhythm off. Reflect Orbital CEO Ben Nowack dismissed these fears to the outlet Payload by saying that some people once feared light bulbs.

“I think a lot of people are scared of new things,” Nowack told Payload. “Similar concerns and fears were brought up when light bulbs were introduced to the world, and people were worried about circadian rhythm and like, is this godly?…I think it’s a sign that we’re doing something that’s really new and really important.”

On October 10, Reflect Orbital conducted a test of its technology near the town of Independence, California. As previously noted, the company doesn’t have any satellites in space yet, so instead they used giant, angled flood lights to mimic what the beam would look like from space and invited search-and-rescue groups to the demonstration. For astronomers, the blinding light confirmed their worst fears. Those fears have only grown since mid-July, when the Federal Communications Commission approved the company’s request to build a demonstration satellite called Earendil-1. The name continues the annoying trend of startups borrowing from The Lord of the Rings for their technologies.

“You might think a space mirror could illuminate a customer’s solar farm or a rescue site while leaving everything else untouched,” Macquarie University astrophysicist Richard de Grijs wrote for The Conversation. “That’s not quite how it works, because Earth’s atmosphere doesn’t respect sharp boundaries.”

A study in The Astrophysical Journal of Letters showed how molecules and aerosols would scatter this reflected sunlight, and another study detailed how a satellite with a 54-meter mirror (which is the operational goal) would still be brighter than our planet’s lone satellite if you were eight miles away from the beam. Within the beam, light would appear 40 times brighter than the moon, and the sky would be as luminous as after-sunset twilight. If Reflect Orbital reaches its planned 50,000-satellite constellation, the night sky would become three to four times brighter overall, according to the European Southern Observatory.

For now, the company is forging ahead with its plan to launch its first satellites with India’s Skyroot Aerospace, which will require authorization with the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre. This means the company could technically sidestep U.S. regulatory approval entirely.

“This whole question we have is: Who owns the night sky?” University of Alabama astronomer Michelle Wooten told Sky & Telescope. “I really feel that people should have a say on what their night sky looks like.”
